questions.text: In the early stages of fetal development, primordial germ cells must migrate from the yolk sac to populate the developing gonads. Once they arrive in the ovarian cortex, what specific cellular process do they immediately undergo to increase their numbers?
options: First meiotic division
Second meiotic division
Rapid mitotic proliferation
Direct differentiation into primary oocytes
questions.correctAnswer: C. Rapid mitotic proliferation
questions.explanation: Upon reaching the ovarian cortex, primordial germ cells (oogonia) undergo rapid mitotic multiplication to significantly increase their population before any meiotic divisions begin.

questions.text: The transition from an oogonium to a primary oocyte is a critical step in prenatal development. By which fetal age do some oogonia enlarge to become primary oocytes and commence the first stage of meiotic division?
options: First and second months
Fourth and fifth months
Seventh and eighth months
Shortly before birth
questions.correctAnswer: B. Fourth and fifth months
questions.explanation: By the fourth and fifth months of human fetal development, some oogonia enlarge, differentiate into primary oocytes, and enter the prophase of their first meiotic division.

questions.text: During the seventh month of fetal development, the primary oocytes become encapsulated. What specific type of cell surrounds a single primary oocyte to form a primordial follicle?
options: A single layer of flattened follicular cells
A stratified layer of cuboidal granulosa cells
A single layer of columnar epithelial cells
A multilayered theca interna
questions.correctAnswer: A. A single layer of flattened follicular cells
questions.explanation: A primordial follicle is characterized by a primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flattened (squamous) follicular cells, which occurs around the seventh month of fetal development.

questions.text: The encapsulation of the primary oocyte to form a primordial follicle has a profound physiological effect on its meiotic progression. What is this effect?
options: It accelerates the completion of the first meiotic division.
It triggers the immediate onset of the second meiotic division.
It arrests the first meiotic division at the diplotene stage of prophase.
It causes the immediate extrusion of the first polar body.
questions.correctAnswer: C. It arrests the first meiotic division at the diplotene stage of prophase.
questions.explanation: The encapsulation by flattened follicular cells arrests the primary oocyte in the diplotene stage of prophase of the first meiotic division, a state that persists until after puberty.

questions.text: At the time of birth, the female ovaries contain a finite reserve of germ cells. Approximately how many primordial follicles are present in the ovaries at birth?
questions.explanation: At birth, a female infant possesses approximately 500,000 primordial follicles, which represents the entire pool of potential ova for her reproductive lifespan.

questions.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis tightly regulates the ovarian cycle. Which hormone, synthesized by the hypothalamus, acts as a simple decapeptide to initiate this cascade?
options: Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)
Luteinizing Hormone (LH)
Gonadotrophin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)
Progesterone
questions.correctAnswer: C. Gonadotrophin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)
questions.explanation: Gonadotrophin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) is a decapeptide secreted by the hypothalamus that travels via the hypophysial portal system to stimulate the anterior pituitary.

questions.text: Gonadotrophin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) exerts its primary effect on which specific anatomical structure to stimulate the release of gonadotrophins?
options: Posterior pituitary gland
Anterior pituitary gland
Theca interna cells of the ovary
Granulosa cells of the ovary
questions.correctAnswer: B. Anterior pituitary gland
questions.explanation: GnRH is transported via the hypophysial portal blood vessels directly to the anterior pituitary gland, where it stimulates the production and release of FSH and LH.

questions.text: The secretion of GnRH by the hypothalamus is subject to a complex feedback mechanism. Which hormones primarily exert this feedback control?
options: FSH and LH
Oestrogen and progesterone
Inhibin and relaxin
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
questions.correctAnswer: B. Oestrogen and progesterone
questions.explanation: The secretion of GnRH is mainly controlled by the circulating levels of ovarian steroids, specifically oestrogen and progesterone, through both negative and positive feedback loops.

questions.text: Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH) are classified biochemically as which type of molecule?
options: Steroids
Simple peptides
Glycoproteins
Catecholamines
questions.correctAnswer: C. Glycoproteins
questions.explanation: Both FSH and LH, produced by the anterior pituitary gland, are biochemically classified as glycoprotein hormones.

questions.text: During the first half of the ovarian cycle, Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) is predominantly responsible for which physiological event?
options: The luteinization of granulosa cells
The rapid growth and maturation of ovarian follicles
The immediate triggering of ovulation
The maintenance of the corpus luteum
questions.correctAnswer: B. The rapid growth and maturation of ovarian follicles
questions.explanation: In the first half of the cycle (follicular phase), FSH is released to act on the ovaries, rescuing 15 to 20 primordial follicles from atresia and stimulating their growth and maturation.

questions.text: Ovulation is a dramatic event triggered by a highly specific hormonal shift. Approximately 24 to 36 hours before ovulation, which phenomenon occurs?
options: A sudden, sharp drop in circulating oestrogen
A massive surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH) release
A sustained plateau of elevated progesterone
Complete suppression of FSH secretion
questions.correctAnswer: B. A massive surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH) release
questions.explanation: The LH surge, a sudden and massive increase in LH released by the anterior pituitary, occurs 24-36 hours prior to ovulation and is the definitive trigger for follicular rupture.

questions.text: Following ovulation, the ruptured follicle undergoes a significant structural and functional transformation. What is the primary role of LH in this specific process?
options: It causes the immediate atresia of the ruptured follicle.
It transforms the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum.
It stimulates the newly formed corpus luteum to secrete only oestrogen.
It prevents the vascularization of the granulosa cells.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It transforms the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum.
questions.explanation: The LH surge not only triggers ovulation but also promotes the luteinization of the remaining granulosa and theca cells, transforming the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum.

questions.text: Oestrogens play a crucial role in driving the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle. Which specific cells within the maturing ovarian follicle are primarily responsible for oestrogen production?
options: Oocytes
Theca cells
Fibroblasts of the theca externa
Endothelial cells of the stromal vasculature
questions.correctAnswer: B. Theca cells
questions.explanation: Oestrogens are primarily produced by the theca cells (specifically theca interna) of maturing ovarian follicles, often in concert with granulosa cells.

questions.text: In the context of the regular 28-day ovarian cycle, at what point do circulating oestrogen levels typically reach their absolute peak?
options: At the onset of menstruation (Day 1)
Approximately two days before ovulation
Exactly at the moment of follicular rupture
During the mid-luteal phase (Day 21)
questions.correctAnswer: B. Approximately two days before ovulation
questions.explanation: Oestrogen levels rise steadily during the follicular phase and reach their peak concentration approximately two days prior to ovulation, subsequently triggering the LH surge via positive feedback.

questions.text: During the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle, oestrogen exerts profound effects on the uterine lining. Which of the following is a direct morphological result of this oestrogenic action?
options: The endometrial stroma progressively thickens and glands elongate.
The endometrial glands become highly tortuous and saccular.
The spiral arteries undergo intense, sustained vasoconstriction.
The stratum basale is completely shed and expelled.
questions.correctAnswer: A. The endometrial stroma progressively thickens and glands elongate.
questions.explanation: Oestrogen acts on the endometrium to initiate repair and proliferation; the stroma thickens, glands elongate but remain relatively straight, and spiral arteries begin to grow toward the surface.

questions.text: Progesterone is the dominant hormone of the luteal phase, preparing the uterus for potential implantation. Which structure is the primary source of progesterone during the non-pregnant ovarian cycle?
options: The maturing Graafian follicle
The corpus luteum
The adrenal cortex
The stratum spongiosum of the endometrium
questions.correctAnswer: B. The corpus luteum
questions.explanation: Progesterone is predominantly produced by the theca-lutein and granulosa-lutein cells that constitute the corpus luteum following ovulation.

questions.text: Working in synergy with oestrogens during the secretory phase, progesterone stimulates the endometrial glands to perform which specific function?
options: To undergo rapid mitotic division to form new crypts
To secrete rich mucoid materials containing abundant glycogen
To break down and release proteolytic enzymes for shedding
To convert from a simple columnar to a stratified squamous epithelium
questions.correctAnswer: B. To secrete rich mucoid materials containing abundant glycogen
questions.explanation: Progesterone causes the newly elongated endometrial glands to widen, become tortuous, and actively secrete a glycogen-rich mucoid material to nourish a potentially implanting blastocyst.

questions.text: Inhibin is a hormone that plays a crucial regulatory role in the ovarian cycle. Which cells are responsible for the production of this non-steroid hormone?
options: Theca interna cells
Luteal cells of the corpus albicans
Granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles
Syncytiotrophoblast cells
questions.correctAnswer: C. Granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles
questions.explanation: Inhibin is produced by the granulosa cells of the developing ovarian follicles.

questions.text: What is the primary physiological target and action of the hormone inhibin during the ovarian cycle?
options: It acts on the endometrium to initiate the secretory phase.
It acts on the anterior pituitary to inhibit the secretion of gonadotrophins.
It acts on the hypothalamus to stimulate GnRH release.
It acts directly on the corpus luteum to prolong its lifespan.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It acts on the anterior pituitary to inhibit the secretion of gonadotrophins.
questions.explanation: Inhibin acts via negative feedback directly on the anterior pituitary gland to suppress the secretion of gonadotrophins, particularly FSH, which contributes to the eventual regression of the corpus luteum.

questions.text: If fertilization and implantation do not occur, the corpus luteum undergoes regression. What is the immediate endocrine consequence of this regression that directly precipitates menstruation?
options: A sudden surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH)
A dramatic fall in blood levels of oestrogen and progesterone
A rapid increase in the production of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
An elevation in hypothalamic GnRH secretion
questions.correctAnswer: B. A dramatic fall in blood levels of oestrogen and progesterone
questions.explanation: The demise of the corpus luteum ceases its production of ovarian steroids, leading to a precipitous drop in circulating oestrogen and progesterone, which triggers the shedding of the endometrial lining.

questions.text: Early in the follicular phase, a cohort of 15 to 20 primordial follicles is recruited to begin maturation. What specific hormonal action rescues these follicles from becoming atretic?
options: Stimulation by Progesterone
Stimulation by Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)
Inhibition by Luteinizing Hormone (LH)
Stimulation by placental oestrogens
questions.correctAnswer: B. Stimulation by Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)
questions.explanation: At the beginning of each cycle, rising levels of FSH rescue a small cohort of 15-20 primordial follicles from programmed cell death (atresia), prompting them to grow.

questions.text: Despite the initial recruitment of multiple follicles, typically only one achieves full maturity to ovulate. What is the fate of the remaining recruited follicles that fail to reach this stage?
options: They revert back to primordial follicles for the next cycle.
They migrate to the contralateral ovary.
They become atretic and are replaced by connective tissue, forming corpus atreticum.
They immediately transform into accessory corpora lutea.
questions.correctAnswer: C. They become atretic and are replaced by connective tissue, forming corpus atreticum.
questions.explanation: The follicles that do not achieve dominance undergo a degenerative process called atresia. They are resorbed and replaced by connective tissue, forming a structure known as corpus atreticum.

questions.text: The transition from a primordial follicle to a primary follicle involves distinct morphological changes in the surrounding epithelial cells. Which description accurately characterizes this change?
options: The cells change from cuboidal to columnar and secrete mucus.
The cells change from flat (squamous) to cuboidal and proliferate to form a stratified layer.
The cells undergo apoptosis to create a fluid-filled cavity.
The cells fuse to form a multinucleated syncytium around the oocyte.
questions.correctAnswer: B. The cells change from flat (squamous) to cuboidal and proliferate to form a stratified layer.
questions.explanation: A primordial follicle becomes a primary follicle when its single layer of flat squamous cells changes to a cuboidal shape and then proliferates to form a stratified epithelium of granulosa cells.

questions.text: As the primary follicle develops, a distinct, thick, homogeneous layer forms between the primary oocyte and the surrounding granulosa cells. What is this layer called?
options: Theca interna
Theca externa
Zona pellucida
Stratum granulosum
questions.correctAnswer: C. Zona pellucida
questions.explanation: The zona pellucida is a thick layer of glycoproteins and acid proteoglycans that develops between the oocyte and the surrounding follicular (granulosa) cells during the primary follicle stage.

questions.text: The stromal cells surrounding the growing primary follicle organize into a specialized capsule known as the theca folliculi. This capsule further differentiates into two layers. What characterizes the theca interna?
options: It is an outer fibrous capsule composed mainly of collagen.
It is an inner layer composed of secretory cells.
It is an avascular layer that merges with the ovarian epithelium.
It is composed exclusively of fluid-filled lacunae.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It is an inner layer composed of secretory cells.
questions.explanation: The theca folliculi organizes into an inner theca interna, which is highly vascularized and composed of glandular, secretory cells, and an outer theca externa, which is a fibrous connective tissue layer.

questions.text: The defining characteristic that marks the transition from a primary follicle to a secondary (antral) follicle is the appearance of which structure?
options: The zona pellucida
The theca externa
Fluid-filled spaces that coalesce to form the antrum
The corona radiata
questions.correctAnswer: C. Fluid-filled spaces that coalesce to form the antrum
questions.explanation: A primary follicle is reclassified as a secondary (vesicular or antral) follicle when fluid-filled spaces develop between the granulosa cells and coalesce to form a single large cavity called the antrum.

questions.text: As the antrum of the secondary follicle enlarges, it displaces the primary oocyte to an eccentric position. However, the oocyte remains surrounded by a mound of intact granulosa cells. What is this specific group of cells termed?
options: Stratum basale
Cumulus oophorus
Theca lutein cells
Corpus albicans
questions.correctAnswer: B. Cumulus oophorus
questions.explanation: The cumulus oophorus is the localized mound of granulosa cells that remains intimately associated with the primary oocyte, anchoring it to the follicular wall as the fluid-filled antrum expands.

questions.text: At its peak of maturation just prior to ovulation, the fully developed secondary follicle is often referred to by a specific eponym. What is this term, and what is its approximate diameter?
options: Primordial follicle; 5 mm
Graafian follicle; 25 mm or more
Corpus atreticum; 10 mm
Theca folliculi; 2 mm
questions.correctAnswer: B. Graafian follicle; 25 mm or more
questions.explanation: A fully mature secondary follicle is commonly called a Graafian follicle (or tertiary/mature follicle) and can reach a diameter of 25 mm or more, forming a visible bulge on the ovarian surface.

questions.text: The preovulatory phase is initiated by the LH surge. During this critical window, what significant nuclear event occurs within the primary oocyte?
options: It replicates its DNA for a second time.
It completely finishes both meiotic divisions.
It completes meiosis I, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body.
It enters a new resting phase known as dictyotene.
questions.correctAnswer: C. It completes meiosis I, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body.
questions.explanation: The LH surge induces the primary oocyte to resume and complete its first meiotic division, resulting in two haploid daughter cells of unequal size: the large secondary oocyte and the tiny first polar body.

questions.text: Following the completion of meiosis I, the newly formed secondary oocyte immediately enters meiosis II. However, it does not complete this division before ovulation. At which specific stage does it arrest?
options: Prophase II
Metaphase II
Anaphase II
Telophase II
questions.correctAnswer: B. Metaphase II
questions.explanation: The secondary oocyte enters meiosis II but arrests at metaphase II approximately 3 hours before ovulation. It will remain in this state until fertilization occurs.

questions.text: What is the primary anatomical location of the first polar body immediately following its formation?
options: Deep within the cytoplasm of the secondary oocyte
Floating freely within the follicular antrum
Between the zona pellucida and the cell membrane of the secondary oocyte
Embedded within the cells of the theca interna
questions.correctAnswer: C. Between the zona pellucida and the cell membrane of the secondary oocyte
questions.explanation: The first polar body is extruded into the perivitelline space, which is the narrow gap located between the plasma membrane of the secondary oocyte and the surrounding zona pellucida.

questions.text: In the hours leading up to ovulation, the high concentration of LH triggers an increase in specific enzymatic activity that weakens the follicular wall. Which enzyme is primarily responsible for digesting the collagen fibers surrounding the follicle?
options: Hyaluronidase
Collagenase
Plasminogen
Acid phosphatase
questions.correctAnswer: B. Collagenase
questions.explanation: The LH surge increases collagenase activity, leading to the digestion of the collagen fibers that provide structural integrity to the follicular wall, preparing it for rupture.

questions.text: Alongside enzymatic digestion, the physical extrusion of the oocyte during ovulation is facilitated by local muscular contractions of the ovarian wall. Which substance, elevated in response to the LH surge, stimulates these contractions?
options: Progesterone
Prostaglandins
Inhibin
Relaxin
questions.correctAnswer: B. Prostaglandins
questions.explanation: The LH surge causes an increase in local prostaglandin levels, which induce rhythmic muscular contractions in the ovarian wall that help physically squeeze and extrude the oocyte from the ruptured follicle.

questions.text: Just prior to ovulation, a localized, avascular bulge appears on the surface of the ovary over the most convex point of the mature follicle. What is the specific anatomical term for this spot?
options: Cumulus oophorus
Corpus luteum
Stigma
Macula lutea
questions.correctAnswer: C. Stigma
questions.explanation: As the follicle prepares to rupture, the overlying stroma and theca cells thin out, and an avascular, nipple-like protrusion called the stigma appears on the ovarian surface.

questions.text: Upon ovulation, the secondary oocyte is expelled along with its zona pellucida and a surrounding layer of specialized granulosa cells. What is the name given to these arranged cells post-ovulation?
options: Theca externa
Stratum compactum
Corona radiata
Corpus albicans
questions.correctAnswer: C. Corona radiata
questions.explanation: After ovulation, the cells of the cumulus oophorus that remain attached to and arranged radially around the zona pellucida of the ovulated oocyte are collectively termed the corona radiata.

questions.text: Immediately following its release from the ovary, the oocyte must be transported into the uterine tube. Which mechanisms are primarily responsible for capturing and moving the oocyte?
options: High-pressure fluid jets from the ruptured follicle
The sweeping movement of the fimbriae and the motion of cilia on the tubal epithelium
Chemotactic attraction by the endometrium
Amoeboid movement of the corona radiata cells
questions.correctAnswer: B. The sweeping movement of the fimbriae and the motion of cilia on the tubal epithelium
questions.explanation: The fimbriae of the uterine tube sweep over the ovary to catch the oocyte, and the beating cilia on the epithelial lining of the tube propel the oocyte slowly toward the uterus.

questions.text: If the secondary oocyte is not successfully fertilized by a spermatozoon, what is its expected viable lifespan within the female reproductive tract?
options: 1 to 2 hours
12 to 24 hours
3 to 4 days
Up to 7 days
questions.correctAnswer: B. 12 to 24 hours
questions.explanation: An unfertilized ovum has a very short viable lifespan; it typically dies and begins to degenerate within 12 to 24 hours after being ovulated.

questions.text: Following ovulation, the remnants of the ruptured follicle (granulosa and theca interna cells) undergo a transformation driven by LH. What is the resulting glandular structure called?
options: Corpus atreticum
Corpus albicans
Corpus luteum
Graafian follicle
questions.correctAnswer: C. Corpus luteum
questions.explanation: The collapsed walls of the ruptured follicle undergo luteinization under the influence of LH, developing yellowish pigment and transforming into the corpus luteum, a temporary endocrine gland.

questions.text: During the formation of the corpus luteum, the granulosa cells acquire a polyhedral shape and their cytoplasm fills with a specific yellow pigment. What is the name of this pigment?
options: Melanin
Bilirubin
Lutein
Lipofuscin
questions.correctAnswer: C. Lutein
questions.explanation: The cells of the corpus luteum accumulate a yellowish lipid-rich pigment called lutein, which gives the structure its characteristic yellow appearance (corpus luteum means "yellow body").

questions.text: To function effectively as an endocrine gland, the newly formed corpus luteum requires a robust blood supply. Where do the invading blood vessels primarily originate from?
options: The tunica albuginea
The theca interna
The adjacent fallopian tube
The peritoneal cavity
questions.correctAnswer: B. The theca interna
questions.explanation: During luteinization, blood vessels originating from the theca interna actively invade the mass of luteal cells, providing the rich vascularization necessary for rapid hormone transport.

questions.text: In the absence of fertilization, the corpus luteum has a strictly limited functional lifespan. What is the maximum duration it typically persists before degenerating?
options: 7 days
14 days
21 days
28 days
questions.correctAnswer: B. 14 days
questions.explanation: If pregnancy does not occur, the "corpus luteum of menstruation" reaches its maximum development and functional capacity approximately 9 to 14 days post-ovulation before it begins to involute.

questions.text: When the corpus luteum of menstruation degenerates, it shrinks and forms a mass of white, fibrotic scar tissue within the ovary. What is the specific anatomical term for this scar?
options: Corpus albicans
Corpus atreticum
Macula densa
Stigma
questions.correctAnswer: A. Corpus albicans
questions.explanation: The degenerated, fibrotic remnant of the corpus luteum is completely devoid of pigment and is therefore called the corpus albicans (meaning "white body").

questions.text: If successful fertilization and implantation occur, the corpus luteum is rescued from degeneration. Which specific hormone is responsible for maintaining the corpus luteum during early pregnancy?
options: High levels of maternal Luteinizing Hormone (LH)
Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) secreted by the embryonic syncytiotrophoblast
Prolactin secreted by the maternal anterior pituitary
Oxytocin secreted by the posterior pituitary
questions.correctAnswer: B. Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) secreted by the embryonic syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: The developing embryo (specifically the syncytiotrophoblast) secretes hCG, an LH-like hormone that signals the corpus luteum to persist and continue producing progesterone, becoming the "corpus luteum of pregnancy."

questions.text: The corpus luteum of pregnancy grows significantly to support the gestation. By the third month of development, approximately what proportion of the total ovarian volume might it occupy?
options: It shrinks entirely by the second month.
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum of pregnancy becomes very large, potentially occupying 1/3 to 1/2 of the entire volume of the ovary by the end of the first trimester, before the placenta fully takes over hormone production.

questions.text: The menstrual cycle specifically describes the cyclical changes occurring in the endometrium. Histologically, the endometrium is divided into three distinct layers. Which layer lies deepest and remains intact during menstruation?
options: Stratum compactum
Stratum spongiosum
Stratum basale
Stratum corneum
questions.correctAnswer: C. Stratum basale
questions.explanation: The stratum basale (basal layer) is the deepest layer, adjacent to the myometrium. It undergoes little change during the cycle, is not shed during menstruation, and serves as the regenerative base for the next cycle.

questions.text: During the secretory phase, the superficial and intermediate layers of the endometrium become highly developed and oedematous. What are these two layers collectively called, reflecting their fate during menstruation?
options: Stratum basale
Stratum germinativum
Stratum functionalis
Stratum lucidum
questions.correctAnswer: C. Stratum functionalis
questions.explanation: The superficial stratum compactum and the intermediate stratum spongiosum undergo dramatic cyclical changes and are both shed during menstruation. Together, they constitute the functional layer, or stratum functionalis.

questions.text: The vascular supply to the endometrium is highly specialized. While straight arteries supply the basal layer, which specific type of arteries supply the stratum functionalis and are highly responsive to hormonal changes?
options: Arcuate arteries
Radial arteries
Spiral arteries
Helicine arteries
questions.correctAnswer: C. Spiral arteries
questions.explanation: The spiral arteries are long, coiled vessels that extend into the compact and spongy layers. They are exquisitely sensitive to progesterone and oestrogen levels, and their constriction initiates the ischemic phase preceding menstruation.

questions.text: The post-menstrual (early proliferative) phase is characterized by regeneration. What is the typical appearance of the uterine glands during this specific phase?
options: They are wide, tortuous, and saccular.
They are straight and beginning to grow in length.
They are completely absent, replaced by dense stroma.
They are actively secreting thick, glycogen-rich mucus.
questions.correctAnswer: B. They are straight and beginning to grow in length.
questions.explanation: Immediately following menstruation, the endometrium is thin. During the early repair phase, the remaining basal portions of the uterine glands simply grow straight upwards to re-epithelialize the surface.

questions.text: The proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle is driven primarily by which hormone, and it parallels which phase of the corresponding ovarian cycle?
options: Driven by progesterone; parallels the luteal phase
Driven by oestrogen; parallels the growth of ovarian follicles
Driven by LH; parallels ovulation
Driven by hCG; parallels corpus luteum regression
questions.correctAnswer: B. Driven by oestrogen; parallels the growth of ovarian follicles
questions.explanation: The proliferative phase is stimulated by rising levels of oestrogen produced by the developing ovarian follicles, therefore it occurs concurrently with the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle.

questions.text: As the secretory phase progresses under the influence of progesterone, the endometrial glands undergo marked morphological changes. Which description accurately reflects the glands during the peak of the secretory phase?
options: They become straight, narrow, and inactive.
They shrink and undergo apoptosis.
They become wide, tortuous, and saccular, filled with secretions.
They transform into solid cords of epithelial cells.
questions.correctAnswer: C. They become wide, tortuous, and saccular, filled with secretions.
questions.explanation: Progesterone induces the glands to become highly coiled, widened (saccular), and actively secrete glycogen-rich material into their lumens to prepare for potential embryo implantation.

questions.text: The sudden withdrawal of which hormone directly causes the intense constriction of the spiral arteries, leading to endometrial ischemia and subsequent menstruation?
options: Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)
Oestrogen
Progesterone
Prolactin
questions.correctAnswer: C. Progesterone
questions.explanation: The regression of the corpus luteum causes a sharp decline in progesterone. The spiral arteries depend on progesterone; its absence causes them to go into sustained spasm, choking off blood supply to the functionalis layer.

questions.text: When the menstrual phase begins, exactly which parts of the endometrium are shed and expelled from the uterus?
options: Only the stratum compactum
The stratum compactum and stratum spongiosum
The stratum spongiosum and stratum basale
The entire endometrium down to the myometrium
questions.correctAnswer: B. The stratum compactum and stratum spongiosum
questions.explanation: Menstruation involves the shedding of the entire stratum functionalis, which comprises both the superficial stratum compactum and the underlying stratum spongiosum, leaving only the stratum basale intact.

questions.text: During normal conception, where does the human blastocyst typically implant within the uterine cavity?
options: In the cervical canal
Deep within the myometrial muscle layer
In the endometrium along the anterior or posterior wall of the body of the uterus
At the extreme fundus, blocking the fallopian tube openings
questions.correctAnswer: C. In the endometrium along the anterior or posterior wall of the body of the uterus
questions.explanation: Normal implantation occurs in the functional layer of the endometrium, most commonly on the anterior or posterior wall of the main body of the uterus.

questions.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are a common method of birth control. Based on the physiology of the ovarian cycle, what is the primary mechanism by which these pills prevent pregnancy?
options: They cause a continuous, unyielding LH surge.
They physically block the fallopian tubes with thickened mucus.
The continuous presence of exogenous progesterone prevents the LH surge, thereby inhibiting ovulation.
They actively destroy primordial follicles within the ovary.
questions.correctAnswer: C. The continuous presence of exogenous progesterone prevents the LH surge, thereby inhibiting ovulation.
questions.explanation: OCPs contain synthetic progestins (and often oestrogens) that provide constant negative feedback to the pituitary. This prevents the mid-cycle LH surge, effectively halting follicular maturation and preventing ovulation.

questions.text: The "rhythm method" of contraception relies on calculating the fertile window. Based on standard gamete viability, fertilization can realistically only occur if intercourse takes place within which specific timeframe relative to ovulation?
options: Between 7 days before and 7 days after ovulation
Between 4 days before ovulation and 2 days after ovulation
Strictly on the exact day of ovulation
Only during the 3 days following ovulation
questions.correctAnswer: B. Between 4 days before ovulation and 2 days after ovulation
questions.explanation: Sperm can survive in the female tract for roughly 4 days, while an ovulated ovum is viable for at most 2 days. Therefore, the fertile window is generally considered to be 4 days prior to and 2 days following ovulation.

questions.text: Some women experience a mild, localized pain in the lower abdomen precisely at the time of ovulation. What is the clinical term often used to describe this phenomenon?
options: Dysmenorrhea
Mittelschmerz (middle pain)
Endometriosis
Pelvic inflammatory disease
questions.correctAnswer: B. Mittelschmerz (middle pain)
questions.explanation: Mittelschmerz, derived from German for "middle pain," refers to the slight, often unilateral abdominal pain some women feel mid-cycle, corresponding to the rupture of the Graafian follicle and release of follicular fluid.

questions.text: Anovulation (failure to ovulate) is a common cause of female infertility. If this condition is due to an insufficient release of pituitary hormones, what medical intervention is most logical?
options: Surgical removal of the corpus albicans
Administration of high-dose continuous progesterone
Administration of an agent to stimulate gonadotrophin release (e.g., clomiphene citrate)
Ligation of the spiral arteries
questions.correctAnswer: C. Administration of an agent to stimulate gonadotrophin release (e.g., clomiphene citrate)
questions.explanation: If anovulation is due to low FSH/LH, administering drugs that stimulate the pituitary to release gonadotrophins (often by blocking oestrogen negative feedback) can successfully induce follicular development and ovulation.

questions.text: If a woman is pregnant but requires surgical removal of her ovaries (oophorectomy) during the second month of gestation, what is the most likely outcome for the pregnancy, and why?
options: The pregnancy will continue normally because the placenta is already fully functional.
Spontaneous abortion will occur because the primary source of progesterone (the corpus luteum) has been removed.
The pregnancy will continue, but the fetus will suffer severe growth restriction.
The uterus will immediately enter a state of tetanic contraction.
questions.correctAnswer: B. Spontaneous abortion will occur because the primary source of progesterone (the corpus luteum) has been removed.
questions.explanation: Before the fourth month, the corpus luteum of pregnancy is the absolute required source of progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining. Removing it before the placenta is capable of producing sufficient progesterone will result in abortion.

questions.text: During the mid-luteal phase of a normal 28-day cycle, which histological feature is most characteristic of the endometrial stroma?
options: It is extremely dense, thin, and highly cellular.
It is entirely avascular and necrotic.
It becomes loose, soft, and distinctly oedematous.
It is replaced completely by stratified squamous epithelium.
questions.correctAnswer: C. It becomes loose, soft, and distinctly oedematous.
questions.explanation: Under the influence of peak progesterone during the secretory (luteal) phase, the endometrial stroma becomes highly vascularized, soft, and oedematous (water-logged) to provide a receptive bed for implantation.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly pairs the phase of the menstrual cycle with its corresponding phase in the ovarian cycle?
options: Menstrual phase corresponds to the Luteal phase.
Proliferative phase corresponds to the Follicular phase.
Secretory phase corresponds to the Follicular phase.
Proliferative phase corresponds to the Luteal phase.
questions.correctAnswer: B. Proliferative phase corresponds to the Follicular phase.
questions.explanation: The proliferative building of the endometrium is driven by oestrogen, which is produced by the growing follicles during the follicular phase of the ovary. Therefore, the proliferative and follicular phases occur simultaneously.

questions.text: During the normal shedding of the endometrium (menstruation), how does the physical process of tissue desquamation typically occur?
options: The entire functional layer detaches instantly as a single, solid cast.
Shedding is gradual, occurring bit by bit over several days.
Only the epithelial lining of the glands is shed, leaving the stroma intact.
Shedding begins at the basal layer and works its way superficially.
questions.correctAnswer: B. Shedding is gradual, occurring bit by bit over several days.
questions.explanation: Menstruation is not a sudden, massive sloughing of tissue. It is a gradual, piece-by-piece breakdown and shedding of the necrotic functional layer over a period of roughly 3 to 5 days.

questions.text: What is the primary function of the stratum basale during the menstrual cycle?
options: To synthesize and secrete large volumes of glycogen-rich mucus
To serve as the primary site of blastocyst implantation
To act as the regenerative layer for rebuilding the glands and arteries after menstruation
To produce progesterone in the absence of a corpus luteum
questions.correctAnswer: C. To act as the regenerative layer for rebuilding the glands and arteries after menstruation
questions.explanation: The stratum basale contains the blind ends of the uterine glands and its own independent blood supply (basal arteries). It survives menstruation and provides the stem cells necessary to regenerate the functional layer.

questions.text: In a standard 28-day cycle, on roughly which day does ovulation typically occur, separating the follicular and luteal phases?
options: Day 7
Day 14
Day 21
Day 28
questions.correctAnswer: B. Day 14
questions.explanation: In an idealized 28-day cycle, the follicular phase lasts about 14 days, culminating in ovulation around Day 14, followed by a relatively constant 14-day luteal phase.

questions.text: During the very late secretory phase, just prior to menstruation, the apical portions of the endometrial glandular epithelial cells undergo a specific change. What happens to them?
options: They undergo rapid, uncontrolled mitosis.
They are shed off as part of their robust apocrine-like secretion process.
They keratinize to protect against ischemic damage.
They fuse to form giant multinucleated cells.
questions.correctAnswer: B. They are shed off as part of their robust apocrine-like secretion process.
questions.explanation: As the glands maximize their secretory activity, the apical (top) parts of the glandular cells are often shed into the lumen along with the secretory product, leaving the cells looking cuboidal with a regular edge.

questions.text: Which structural component of the ovary is composed of connective tissue and physically separates the granulosa cells of a developing follicle from the surrounding vascularized ovarian stroma?
options: The zona pellucida
The cumulus oophorus
The basement membrane (theca folliculi boundary)
The corona radiata
questions.correctAnswer: C. The basement membrane (theca folliculi boundary)
questions.explanation: The granulosa cells rest on a distinct basement membrane that physically separates the avascular granulosa layer from the highly vascularized theca interna and surrounding ovarian stroma.

questions.text: The production of oestrogen by the growing follicle requires cooperation between two cell types. FSH stimulates the theca cells to produce androgens (like testosterone). What do the granulosa cells do with these androgens?
options: They store them indefinitely in the follicular antrum.
They convert them into progesterone via 5-alpha reductase.
They convert them into oestrogen via the enzyme aromatase.
They secrete them directly into the peritoneal cavity to trigger fimbrial sweeping.
questions.correctAnswer: C. They convert them into oestrogen via the enzyme aromatase.
questions.explanation: Theca cells produce androgens under LH stimulation. These androgens diffuse across the basement membrane into the granulosa cells, which, under FSH stimulation, use aromatase to convert them into oestrogens.

questions.text: As ovulation approaches, the character of the cervical mucus changes significantly. What change occurs, and what is its physiological purpose?
options: It becomes thick and highly acidic to kill invading bacteria.
It undergoes significant thinning to allow for the easier passage of spermatozoa.
It forms a solid plug to prevent the oocyte from falling out.
It becomes completely dehydrated and powdery.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It undergoes significant thinning to allow for the easier passage of spermatozoa.
questions.explanation: High levels of oestrogen just prior to ovulation cause the cervical mucus to become thin, watery, and stringy (spinnbarkeit), creating ideal channels for sperm to swim through the cervix.

questions.text: Immediately following ovulation, the secondary oocyte is in the uterine tube. At this precise moment, what surrounds the zona pellucida?
options: Nothing; it is completely bare.
The entire, intact Graafian follicle
The theca interna and externa layers
The corona radiata
questions.correctAnswer: D. The corona radiata
questions.explanation: The ovulated secondary oocyte takes a layer of cumulus oophorus cells with it. Once free-floating, these radially arranged cells immediately surrounding the zona pellucida are called the corona radiata.

questions.text: What is the primary visual characteristic used by embryologists to identify a secondary (antral) follicle in a histological section of an ovary?
options: A completely bare oocyte lacking a zona pellucida
A single layer of flat squamous cells
The presence of a fluid-filled cavity called an antrum
The presence of a large, highly folded yellow scar
questions.correctAnswer: C. The presence of a fluid-filled cavity called an antrum
questions.explanation: The defining morphological feature that distinguishes a secondary follicle from a primary follicle is the presence of the antrum, formed by the coalescence of fluid-filled spaces among the granulosa cells.

questions.text: If a woman has a regular 32-day menstrual cycle, on approximately which day is she most likely to ovulate?
options: Day 14
Day 16
Day 18
Day 20
questions.correctAnswer: C. Day 18
questions.explanation: While the follicular phase can vary in length, the luteal phase (from ovulation to menstruation) is relatively constant at 14 days. Therefore, in a 32-day cycle, ovulation occurs around Day 18 (32 - 14 = 18).

questions.text: During the proliferative phase, the endometrium responds to oestrogen. Which of the following best describes the state of the spiral arteries during this specific phase?
options: They are rapidly degenerating and bleeding.
They are tightly coiled and undergoing severe spasms.
They are actively growing in length towards the epithelial surface.
They are completely absent, replaced by large venous lakes.
questions.correctAnswer: C. They are actively growing in length towards the epithelial surface.
questions.explanation: In the proliferative phase, as the stroma thickens, the spiral arteries are actively lengthening and growing upward through the newly forming tissue to re-establish the vascular network.

questions.text: The luteal phase is characterized by the dominance of progesterone. Besides its effects on the endometrium, what is a key systemic physiological effect of progesterone that can be measured clinically?
options: A significant drop in blood pressure
A mild but measurable rise in basal body temperature
Complete suppression of all respiratory drive
A massive increase in bone density within hours
questions.correctAnswer: B. A mild but measurable rise in basal body temperature
questions.explanation: Progesterone is thermogenic. Following ovulation, the increased production of progesterone by the corpus luteum causes a slight but reliable increase in basal body temperature (about 0.5°F to 1.0°F).

questions.text: Which of the following cellular structures is specifically responsible for preventing the primary oocyte from completing meiosis I during the long dictyotene resting phase of childhood?
options: The zona pellucida
The theca externa
Oocyte Maturation Inhibitor (OMI) produced by follicular cells
High levels of maternal hCG
questions.correctAnswer: C. Oocyte Maturation Inhibitor (OMI) produced by follicular cells
questions.explanation: The follicular cells surrounding the primary oocyte secrete Oocyte Maturation Inhibitor (OMI), a small peptide that actively maintains the meiotic arrest at the diplotene stage until puberty.

questions.text: As the Graafian follicle matures, it produces large amounts of fluid. What is the composition and clinical name of this fluid that fills the antrum?
options: Amniotic fluid
Liquor folliculi
Cerebrospinal fluid
Ascitic fluid
questions.correctAnswer: B. Liquor folliculi
questions.explanation: The fluid that accumulates in the antrum of the secondary and tertiary (Graafian) follicles is a protein-rich exudate containing high concentrations of hormones (oestrogen), termed liquor folliculi.

questions.text: The theca interna is highly vascularized, whereas the granulosa cell layer in a growing follicle is entirely avascular. How do the granulosa cells receive nutrients and oxygen?
options: Via direct capillary networks that pierce the basement membrane
By phagocytosing the primary oocyte
By diffusion across the basement membrane from the vessels in the theca interna
They do not require oxygen until after ovulation.
questions.correctAnswer: C. By diffusion across the basement membrane from the vessels in the theca interna
questions.explanation: Because the granulosa layer lacks its own blood vessels prior to ovulation, all nutrients, oxygen, and hormones must diffuse from the rich capillary beds of the theca interna across the basement membrane.

questions.text: When does the secondary oocyte finally complete its second meiotic division?
options: At the exact moment of the LH surge
During its transit through the fimbriae
Only if and when it is successfully penetrated by a spermatozoon
Exactly 24 hours after it implants in the uterus
questions.correctAnswer: C. Only if and when it is successfully penetrated by a spermatozoon
questions.explanation: The secondary oocyte remains arrested in metaphase II. The mechanical and chemical events of fertilization (sperm penetration) provide the necessary stimulus for the oocyte to finally complete meiosis II.

questions.text: What is the genetic and cellular consequence when the secondary oocyte completes meiosis II upon fertilization?
options: It forms two identical, functional ova.
It forms a diploid zygote and a second polar body.
It forms a mature haploid ovum and extrudes the second polar body.
It immediately begins rapid mitotic cleavage before fusion.
questions.correctAnswer: C. It forms a mature haploid ovum and extrudes the second polar body.
questions.explanation: Completion of meiosis II results in the unequal division of cytoplasm, creating one large, mature haploid ovum (whose nucleus will become the female pronucleus) and one small, non-functional second polar body.

questions.text: The corpus luteum requires continuous hormonal support to survive past 14 days. In early pregnancy, how does human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) function to provide this support?
options: It binds to FSH receptors to stimulate new follicle growth.
It acts as an analogue of LH, binding to LH receptors on luteal cells to maintain their secretory activity.
It acts as an analogue of oestrogen to stimulate the endometrium directly.
It suppresses the maternal immune system to prevent rejection of the ovary.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It acts as an analogue of LH, binding to LH receptors on luteal cells to maintain their secretory activity.
questions.explanation: hCG is structurally and functionally very similar to pituitary LH. It binds to LH receptors on the corpus luteum, preventing its degeneration and ensuring continuous progesterone production.

questions.text: During the ischemic phase that immediately precedes menstruation, what is the primary cause of the extensive tissue necrosis in the stratum functionalis?
options: Over-proliferation of glands leading to cellular crowding and death
Direct toxic damage from high levels of oestrogen
Spasmodic constriction of the spiral arteries cutting off oxygen and nutrients
Autoimmune attack by maternal macrophages
questions.correctAnswer: C. Spasmodic constriction of the spiral arteries cutting off oxygen and nutrients
questions.explanation: The withdrawal of progesterone causes the spiral arteries to undergo intense, prolonged spasms. This ischemia starves the functional layer of oxygen and nutrients, leading to rapid necrosis and subsequent sloughing.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of the fimbriae during the ovarian cycle?
options: They secrete enzymes to dissolve the ovarian capsule.
They rhythmically sweep over the ovary near the time of ovulation to capture the extruded oocyte.
They produce the LH surge via localized endocrine signaling.
They form a tight seal over the cervix to prevent sperm entry.
questions.correctAnswer: B. They rhythmically sweep over the ovary near the time of ovulation to capture the extruded oocyte.
questions.explanation: The fimbriae are finger-like projections at the end of the fallopian tube. Near ovulation, they become engorged and actively sweep the surface of the ovary to catch the oocyte and guide it into the ostium.

questions.text: By the fifth month of fetal development, the ovaries contain their maximum number of germ cells. Approximately how many germ cells are estimated to be present at this peak?
options: 2 million
7 million
100 million
questions.correctAnswer: C. 7 million
questions.explanation: The population of germ cells peaks at roughly 7 million around the 5th month in utero. After this point, massive atresia begins, drastically reducing the number by birth.

questions.text: Which statement accurately describes the continuous developmental timeline of oogenesis compared to spermatogenesis?
options: Oogenesis is a rapid, continuous process taking roughly 64 days from start to finish.
Both processes remain completely dormant until the onset of puberty.
Oogenesis is highly discontinuous, featuring prolonged arrests spanning from fetal life to potentially decades later.
Oogenesis begins at puberty and ends only at death.
questions.correctAnswer: C. Oogenesis is highly discontinuous, featuring prolonged arrests spanning from fetal life to potentially decades later.
questions.explanation: A hallmark of oogenesis is its extreme discontinuity. It halts in prophase I during fetal life, remains dormant for years, resumes at ovulation, and halts again in metaphase II, only finishing if fertilized.

questions.text: Atretic follicles are those that have undergone degeneration. What is the ultimate fate of the space previously occupied by a large atretic follicle in the ovary?
options: It remains as a permanent fluid-filled cyst.
It is replaced by fibrous connective tissue, leaving a minor scar.
It transforms into a hyperactive endocrine gland.
It fills with blood to form a corpus hemorrhagicum.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It is replaced by fibrous connective tissue, leaving a minor scar.
questions.explanation: When follicles undergo atresia, the oocyte and granulosa cells die and are resorbed. The remaining cavity is invaded by fibroblasts and replaced by connective tissue, forming a small scar (corpus atreticum).

questions.text: During the late secretory phase, the endometrium reaches its maximum thickness. What is the typical physical thickness of a fully developed secretory endometrium?
options: 1 - 2 mm
5 - 7 mm
questions.correctAnswer: B. 5 - 7 mm
questions.explanation: Under the combined influence of oestrogen and high levels of progesterone, the fully succulent, oedematous endometrium during the secretory phase typically reaches a maximum thickness of about 5 to 7 mm.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a morphological characteristic of the endometrial glands during the secretory phase?
options: They are highly tortuous (coiled).
They appear "saw-toothed" in histological section.
They are actively secreting a glycogen-rich fluid.
They are short, straight, and lined by simple cuboidal epithelium.
questions.correctAnswer: D. They are short, straight, and lined by simple cuboidal epithelium.
questions.explanation: Short, straight glands lined by cuboidal cells are characteristic of the early proliferative (post-menstrual) phase. During the secretory phase, glands are highly coiled, widened, and actively secreting.

questions.text: The corpus luteum produces hormones that exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. Which specific hormone combination is primarily responsible for suppressing new follicular development during the luteal phase?
options: High FSH and low LH
High oestrogen and high progesterone
Low inhibin and high GnRH
High oxytocin and low prolactin
questions.correctAnswer: B. High oestrogen and high progesterone
questions.explanation: The high levels of progesterone (working synergistically with oestrogen) produced by the corpus luteum strongly inhibit the release of GnRH, FSH, and LH, preventing any new follicles from maturing while the current cycle concludes.

questions.text: In a histological preparation of an ovary, you observe a large follicle with a vast fluid-filled cavity. The oocyte is pushed to one side, surrounded by a distinct mound of cells. The most appropriate classification for this structure is a:
options: Primordial follicle
Primary follicle
Pre-antral follicle
Graafian (tertiary) follicle
questions.correctAnswer: D. Graafian (tertiary) follicle
questions.explanation: A very large, single fluid-filled cavity (antrum) with the oocyte displaced eccentrically within the cumulus oophorus is the classic histological appearance of a fully mature Graafian (tertiary) follicle.

questions.text: What happens to the first polar body after it is extruded into the perivitelline space?
options: It rapidly enlarges to become a second functional ovum.
It fuses back with the secondary oocyte to restore diploidy.
It often undergoes a second meiotic division but ultimately degenerates.
It secretes hormones to maintain the corpus luteum.
questions.correctAnswer: C. It often undergoes a second meiotic division but ultimately degenerates.
questions.explanation: The first polar body is non-functional due to its lack of cytoplasm. While it may occasionally undergo a second division (resulting in a total of three polar bodies), it inevitably fragments and degenerates.

questions.text: A patient is prescribed clomiphene citrate for infertility. This drug works by blocking oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, deceiving it into sensing low oestrogen levels. What is the expected physiological result on the ovarian cycle?
options: Immediate regression of all developing follicles
Increased GnRH release leading to increased FSH and the potential maturation of multiple follicles
Premature menstruation due to spiral artery spasm
Permanent suppression of the LH surge
questions.correctAnswer: B. Increased GnRH release leading to increased FSH and the potential maturation of multiple follicles
questions.explanation: By blocking the negative feedback of oestrogen, clomiphene causes the hypothalamus to increase GnRH, which increases pituitary FSH secretion. This strong FSH drive can rescue multiple follicles from atresia, leading to superovulation.

questions.text: During the ischemic phase, the spiral arteries constrict. However, blood eventually escapes into the endometrial stroma just before shedding begins. Why does this occur?
options: The spiral arteries rupture due to sudden, massive hypertension.
The spiral arteries undergo brief periods of relaxation, allowing blood to rush into the damaged, necrotic vessels, which then leak.
The straight arteries of the basal layer extend upward and hemorrhage.
The myometrium contracts violently, crushing the superficial vessels.
questions.correctAnswer: B. The spiral arteries undergo brief periods of relaxation, allowing blood to rush into the damaged, necrotic vessels, which then leak.
questions.explanation: After prolonged constriction, the spiral arteries briefly open up (relax). Blood rushes into the ischemic, damaged capillary beds, which easily rupture, leading to diapedesis of red blood cells into the stroma and subsequent sloughing.

questions.text: Which component of the blastocyst is directly responsible for synthesizing and secreting human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) to rescue the corpus luteum?
options: The inner cell mass
The cytotrophoblast
The syncytiotrophoblast
The amniotic epithelium
questions.correctAnswer: C. The syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: Shortly after implantation, the highly invasive, multinucleated outer layer of the trophoblast—the syncytiotrophoblast—begins secreting significant amounts of hCG into the maternal circulation.

questions.text: If the corpus luteum of pregnancy is successfully maintained, until approximately what point in gestation does it serve as the primary, indispensable source of progesterone?
options: Until the end of the first week
Until the end of the fourth month
Until the end of the eighth month
It remains the sole source until parturition.
questions.correctAnswer: B. Until the end of the fourth month
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum of pregnancy is critical for maintaining the endometrium during the first trimester. By the end of the fourth month (roughly 16 weeks), the placenta is large and developed enough to synthesize sufficient progesterone on its own.

questions.text: The basal layer (stratum basale) of the endometrium receives its blood supply from which specific vessels, allowing it to survive the ischemic phase?
options: Spiral arteries
Arcuate arteries
Straight (basal) arteries
Uterine arteries directly
questions.correctAnswer: C. Straight (basal) arteries
questions.explanation: The straight (or basal) arteries are short branches that supply only the stratum basale. Unlike the spiral arteries, they do not possess receptors that make them sensitive to progesterone withdrawal, so they remain patent during menstruation.

questions.text: In the context of the menstrual cycle, the term "diapedesis" refers to which specific event occurring in the endometrium?
options: The active secretion of glycogen by the uterine glands
The escape of red blood cells from damaged superficial vessels into the surrounding stroma
The migration of the blastocyst through the epithelial lining
The rapid mitosis of stromal cells during the proliferative phase
questions.correctAnswer: B. The escape of red blood cells from damaged superficial vessels into the surrounding stroma
questions.explanation: As the ischemic phase transitions into the menstrual phase, damaged vessels leak, and there is an extensive diapedesis (extravasation or escape) of red blood cells into the spongy layer of the endometrium just prior to shedding.

questions.text: During the formation of a primary follicle, the surrounding epithelial cells change shape and begin to proliferate. From what embryological source are these original flat epithelial cells derived?
options: The neural crest
The paraxial mesoderm
The surface (coelomic) epithelium of the ovary
The endoderm of the yolk sac
questions.correctAnswer: C. The surface (coelomic) epithelium of the ovary
questions.explanation: The flat follicular cells that organize around the migrating primordial germ cells to form primordial follicles are derived from the surface epithelium covering the developing fetal ovary (which originates from the coelomic epithelium).

questions.text: The structure of a mature Graafian follicle includes a connective tissue layer called the theca externa. What is the primary characteristic of this specific layer?
options: It is composed of highly active steroid-secreting cells.
It is a dense, fibrous capsule containing fibroblast-like cells that merges with the ovarian stroma.
It forms the immediate, acellular barrier around the oocyte.
It is the layer that directly produces the liquor folliculi.
questions.correctAnswer: B. It is a dense, fibrous capsule containing fibroblast-like cells that merges with the ovarian stroma.
questions.explanation: The theca externa is the outermost layer of the follicular capsule. It is primarily structural, consisting of fibrous connective tissue and smooth muscle-like cells that blend seamlessly into the surrounding ovarian stroma.

questions.text: During the proliferative phase, the epithelial cells lining the uterine glands exhibit a specific morphological change as they prepare for the secretory phase. What is this change?
options: They accumulate lipid droplets at their apical surface.
They accumulate glycogen in their basal portion, which pushes the nucleus closer to the lumen.
They develop dense fields of stereocilia.
They undergo keratinization to protect against the impending blastocyst invasion.
questions.correctAnswer: B. They accumulate glycogen in their basal portion, which pushes the nucleus closer to the lumen.
questions.explanation: As the proliferative phase ends and transitions into the secretory phase, the tall columnar cells of the glands begin to accumulate large amounts of glycogen at their bases, physically displacing the nucleus upward toward the glandular lumen.

questions.text: Which layer of the endometrium is described as having a "compact stromal appearance" and is located most superficially, adjacent to the uterine cavity?
options: Stratum basale
Stratum spongiosum
Stratum compactum
Myometrium
questions.correctAnswer: C. Stratum compactum
questions.explanation: The stratum compactum is the thin, most superficial layer of the endometrium. It gets its name from the densely packed nature of the stromal cells surrounding the narrow necks of the uterine glands in this region.

questions.text: The intermediate layer of the endometrium, the stratum spongiosum, derives its "spongy" appearance primarily from which anatomical feature during the secretory phase?
options: Large, empty air pockets within the tissue
The presence of highly dilated, tortuous, and secretion-filled uterine glands
A dense network of interlocking collagen fibers
Severe, generalized atrophy of the stromal cells
questions.correctAnswer: B. The presence of highly dilated, tortuous, and secretion-filled uterine glands
questions.explanation: During the secretory phase, the uterine glands become highly coiled, dilated, and saccular. When viewed in histological section, these large, winding glandular spaces give the middle layer of the endometrium a porous, "spongy" look.

questions.text: A 28-year-old woman with a consistent 28-day menstrual cycle is charting her basal body temperature. She notices a sustained temperature increase starting on Day 15. This thermal shift is a direct systemic indicator of which recent physiological event?
options: The onset of menses
The peak of the oestrogen surge
The rupture of the follicle and formation of the corpus luteum
The implantation of a blastocyst
questions.correctAnswer: C. The rupture of the follicle and formation of the corpus luteum
questions.explanation: The slight but sustained rise in basal body temperature is caused by the thermogenic effect of progesterone. Because progesterone is secreted by the newly formed corpus luteum, the temperature shift is a reliable retrospective indicator that ovulation has occurred.
